A2.text:
Elvin is a science teacher in Baku. He really loves space. Last week, he bought a very big, expensive telescope. He wanted to see a rare green comet in orbit.

On Saturday, Elvin took his friend Leyla to the mountains in Quba. The night sky in Quba is very dark, so it is perfect for looking at stars. Elvin put his heavy telescope on the grass. He connected it to his laptop and his camera.

“This is a very important experiment,” Elvin said. “I want to take a perfect photo of the Andromeda galaxy tonight.”

Leyla smiled and drank her tea. “You always reach for the stars, Elvin.”

Elvin typed fast on his computer. He waited for the comet to launch into the dark sky. But suddenly, the heavy telescope fell down. Gravity pulled it into the soft mud.

“Oh no!” Elvin shouted. “My computer cannot see the stars now. The camera is dirty. We missed the big discovery!”

He was very sad. He tried to clean the mud off the glass.

Leyla did not look at the computer. She just looked up at the beautiful sky. She pointed her finger.

“Elvin, look,” she said.

Elvin looked up. The green comet was very big and bright. They did not need a computer to see it.

B1.text:
Elvin, a physics teacher from Baku, was obsessed with space. Last week, he spent his entire salary on a high-tech telescope. He wanted to photograph a rare green comet passing through Earth’s orbit.

On Saturday evening, Elvin and his friend Leyla drove up to the mountains in Quba. The sky there is completely clear of city lights. Elvin spent two hours setting up his equipment. He connected wires, attached a heavy camera, and typed numbers into his laptop.

“My hypothesis is that the comet will be visible exactly at midnight,” Elvin explained, adjusting a lens. “This is a serious experiment. We might even see a new galaxy.”

Leyla sat in a camping chair, sipping tea. “You always reach for the stars, Elvin. But I think you are making this too complicated. It isn't rocket science.”

“Technology is important for a true discovery,” he replied proudly.

At five minutes to midnight, Elvin prepared to launch his tracking software. He pressed a button, but he forgot to lock the tripod. Suddenly, gravity did its job. The heavy telescope tipped over and crashed into the soft, wet mud.

“No!” Elvin cried out in panic. He picked up the telescope, but the expensive lens was covered in thick dirt. “The software is running, but the screen is totally dark. The night is ruined!”

He frantically searched for a cleaning cloth in his bag, feeling completely defeated.

Leyla did not panic. She simply stood up, walked away from the laptops, and looked at the sky. She tapped Elvin on the shoulder and pointed up.

“Look,” she said quietly.

Elvin looked up from his messy equipment. There, shining brightly across the dark sky, was the green comet. It was light-years ahead of anything on his computer screen. Sometimes, the best way to look at the universe is just to open your eyes.

B2.text:
Elvin, a physics teacher from Baku, possessed a lifelong obsession with the cosmos. Last week, he emptied his savings account to purchase a state-of-the-art motorized telescope. His ultimate goal was to photograph a rare green comet currently sweeping through Earth’s orbit.

On Saturday evening, Elvin and his friend Leyla drove up to a remote plateau in Quba, far from the light pollution of the capital. While Leyla comfortably settled into a camping chair with a thermos of thyme tea, Elvin spent two agonizing hours assembling his gear. He connected cables, calibrated a heavy digital camera, and frantically typed coordinates into his laptop.

“My working hypothesis is that the comet will peak exactly at midnight,” Elvin muttered, adjusting a delicate lens. “If this experiment works, we might even capture the edge of a distant galaxy.”

Leyla watched him tangling himself in wires and chuckled. “You always reach for the stars, Elvin. But aren't you overcomplicating things? Stargazing isn't exactly rocket science.”

“Precision is crucial for a genuine discovery,” he countered defensively. “My tracking software is light-years ahead of normal observation.”

At five minutes to midnight, Elvin prepared to launch the automated tracking program. He dramatically hit the enter key, entirely forgetting to lock the tripod’s main hinge. Inevitably, gravity took over. The top-heavy telescope tilted forward and face-planted directly into a patch of wet mud.

“Disaster!” Elvin gasped, falling to his knees. He hauled the device upright, but the delicate lens was caked in thick, dark sludge. “The software is running, but the feed is pitch black! I’ve ruined the whole expedition.”

He began frantically digging through his backpack for a microfiber cloth, cursing his own clumsiness.

Leyla, however, remained entirely unbothered by the technological meltdown. She simply stood up, stepped away from the glowing screens, and tilted her head back. After a moment, she tapped her panicked friend on the shoulder and pointed toward the horizon.

“Forget the camera, Elvin,” she said softly.

Elvin abandoned his cloth and looked up. Stretching brilliantly across the velvet sky was the glowing tail of the green comet. It was breathtakingly clear to the naked eye, proving that sometimes the universe doesn't require a machine to be admired.

questions.q: What is the central theme of the narrative?
options: The financial dangers of buying expensive scientific equipment
The importance of traveling to remote areas for safety
How to properly calibrate a motorized telescope
Missing the big picture while focusing too much on technical details
questions.why: Elvin is so focused on his complicated software and gear that he almost misses the comet, which is easily visible just by looking up.

questions.q: Why did Elvin and Leyla choose to go to a remote plateau in Quba?
options: Because the mud there is softer for the tripod
Because Leyla wanted to drink tea in the mountains
To escape the strong winds in Baku
To avoid the light pollution of the capital
questions.why: They drove to Quba to be “far from the light pollution of the capital.”

questions.q: What exactly caused the telescope to fall into the mud?
options: Elvin forgot to lock the main hinge of the tripod
A sudden gust of wind blew it over
Leyla accidentally kicked the power cable
The digital camera was too heavy for the mount
questions.why: “He dramatically hit the enter key, entirely forgetting to lock the tripod’s main hinge.”

questions.q: Elvin managed to clean the lens before the comet disappeared.
options: True
False
Not given
questions.why: He never cleaned it; when Leyla spoke to him, “Elvin abandoned his cloth and looked up.”

questions.q: Elvin claims his software is “light-years ahead” of normal observation. What does this phrase mean?
options: It moves very fast through space
It uses actual starlight to power itself
It takes many years to load properly
It is far more advanced or superior
questions.why: The idiom means something is much more advanced than its competitors or alternatives.

questions.q: What does Leyla's reaction to the “technological meltdown” suggest about her personality?
options: She is completely ignorant about basic astronomy
She prefers simple, direct experiences over complex technology
She enjoys seeing Elvin fail at his experiments
She is impatient and just wants to go home
questions.why: She is unbothered by the broken tech, steps away from the screens, and simply looks up to enjoy the sky.

before.predict: What can you see in the night sky from your home? Guess: who bought a telescope this week — Leyla or Sam?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is science and space. And I did something new this week — I bought a telescope!
[laugh] A real one? Where do you keep it?
On my tiny balcony. On Friday night I looked at the Moon, and then I found Jupiter. You can even see four of its moons as little dots.
That's amazing. Did you see anything further away?
One thing — Andromeda. It looks like a small grey cloud, but it's a whole galaxy with billions of stars. It made me feel very small.
My niece Aysu would love that. She's ten, and last week she did an experiment for school.
Ooh, what kind?
She dropped a heavy book and a light pencil from the table at the same time. Her hypothesis was that the book would land first.
And?
They landed together! That's gravity. Heavy or light, things fall at almost the same speed. She was so excited about her discovery that she told the whole family at dinner.
[chuckle] A future scientist. Is she good at maths?
She says maths is hard, but I tell her it isn't rocket science. Well — sometimes it is rocket science!
Speaking of rockets — did you know Azerbaijan has its own satellites in orbit around the Earth?
Yes! The first one went up in 2013. I watched the launch on TV with my dad. We were so proud.
I love that. Some people say space is a waste of money. What do you think?
I disagree. Space technology gives us weather forecasts, maps on our phones, internet in villages. In some ways, space science is light-years ahead of everything else.
True. And the big new telescopes send us pictures of stars that are older than the Earth.
When I was a child, I wanted to be an astronaut. My teacher always said, "Reach for the stars, Leyla."
And now you talk about the stars on a podcast. That's close enough!
[laugh] Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: would you like to travel to space one day — why or why not?
I'd go, but only if I can take my telescope. See you next time!
Bye for now!
